metadata.title: The Line In The Sand For AVGO Stock

content.text:
A semiconductor giant has fallen back to a familiar battleground, forcing investors to ask if the past is any guide to the future.
Broadcom (AVGO) stock has pulled back, trading around $362.48 after a roughly 15% slide from its one-month high. For watchers of this semiconductor and software powerhouse, the price is less important than the place. The stock now sits in a price zone buyers have defended vigorously three times before. History says buyers show up here. The question every investor must now answer is: will they this time?
The table of prior bounces shows a strong pattern of defense. When tested, this level has served as a launchpad, not merely a defensive floor. The rebounds have varied in character, from a swift 9.3% gain in just 16 days to a more powerful 30% surge that took 53 days to peak. On average, holding this floor has led to a 14.5% gain.
What Happened the Last Three Times Buyers Stepped In?
The historical precedent is clear. In September 2025, buyers absorbed the selling pressure, sparking a 4.6% rally over the next 49 days. They returned just two months later in November, triggering a faster 9.3% pop in only 16 days. The most recent defense, in April 2026, was the most potent, delivering a 30% return to its subsequent peak.
This track record creates a powerful psychological anchor. It's a level where, in recent memory, the risk-reward calculation has tilted decisively in favor of the bulls. But a support level is only a memory of a business, not a guarantee for the one that exists today.
Is This the Same Broadcom Arriving at the Floor?
The company arriving at this level today is, by several measures, far stronger. Trailing twelve-month revenue growth stands at 32%, and the engine for that is artificial intelligence. AI semiconductor revenue hit a record $10.8 billion in the last reported quarter, a 143% year-over-year jump. Management's guidance for Q3 sees that accelerating, forecasting AI semiconductor revenue of $16 billion. Bookings for these chips were over $30 billion in a single quarter, giving the company visibility that it says "runs all the way to 2028 right now."
But here is the honest catch, the potential crack in the floor. The very AI growth driving the business is also pressuring its profitability profile. Management has noted that custom silicon like its TPUs carries lower margins. As this business segment grows, it changes the company's overall mix. For investors who prefer a broader exposure to the industry, a semiconductor ETF like SOXQ offers an alternative. The company's own guidance for Q3 anticipates consolidated gross margin will be down to approximately 74%. As one analyst noted on the recent earnings call, it seems like "gross margin is falling a little bit harder."
